title: Chapter 4 — Legislating Families as Cultural
paragraphs: Chapter 4 moves to New Zealand and asks what happens when a government tries to legislate culture directly. The 1989 Children, Young Persons, and Their Families Act was written after Māori and Pacific Islanders condemned the original bill as too Eurocentric; its signature innovation, the Family Group Conference, was believed to be modelled on Māori and Pacific ways of resolving family conflict. Yet nine years later Samoan social workers still told Gershon they had to "raise the family to the level of the Act" and reshape the Act to fit Samoan families. Why does a law designed to be culturally sensitive still misfit?

Her answer: the Act smuggles in a nuclear-family model disguised as neutral, acultural common sense. It presumes an egalitarian, transparent circulation of knowledge and resources, and treats the parent-child bond as the template relationship. Samoan social workers were not just translating language; they had to take implicit, unspoken parts of Samoan family life and make them explicit topics for conflict resolution — while pushing back against the Act's nuclear-family assumptions.

To show what the Act misses, Gershon documents a kinship shift caused by migration. In Samoa the relationship that models the whole social order is the sister-brother tie (feagaiga), marked by respect and avoidance. In diaspora that tie lapses — siblings share clothes and discuss their love lives — and the relationship that replaces it as the vehicle for "being Samoan" is the parent-child relationship, now the main channel for passing on cultural knowledge and managing resources such as contributions to fa’alavelave.

Both the state and Samoan migrants center the parent-child bond, but for opposite reasons. For the government, the family exists to socialize children into independent, productive citizens; the parent-child hierarchy is temporary, something the child grows out of toward equality. For Samoans the emphasis is outward: children are raised to contribute to the family's connections with other families and communities, not to become independent individuals — independence, from a Samoan view, courts a destructive assimilation. The same relationship encodes opposite projects.

Gershon reads parliamentary debates to show legislators knew that words like "family" and "community" are strategically deployed shifters whose meaning changes by context, and one MP even noted the Crown can only relate to a group by defining it, and in defining almost always misrepresents it. The Act deliberately left "family" vague. Yet MPs still assumed all families share common aims and are unities in which information and resources circulate equally — so family conflict reads as dysfunction. That is the nuclear-family lens applied to extended families.

Two cases seal the argument. The Family Group Conference presumes an originary equality and transparent information flow — the opposite of Samoan family meetings, which exist precisely to assert and contest hierarchy. And the case of Rita, whose three children were removed one by one: her counselor Lupe judged her "not a bad mother, just unsophisticated" — she met the children's physical needs but "acted like their older sister, not their mother." As the eldest sibling in New Zealand with no older relatives, Rita had to carry the whole parental load alone; her younger sister, breaching hierarchy, arranged a visit directly with the worker, and Lupe negotiated Christmas plans with everyone except Rita. By presenting the child-paramount nuclear model as acultural, the Act hid its own cultural presuppositions — and Samoan community workers, by insisting on bringing the Act and the families "onto the same level," were in effect re-marking the acultural as cultural.
